headline: Nature's Own Cure: Rattlesnake Blood Holds Key to Better Snakebite Treatment
meta_description: University of Maryland researchers found that proteins in rattlesnake blood create an antivenom 10 times more potent than current treatments, offering hope for…
summary_short: Scientists discovered that rattlesnakes' natural venom defenses can be combined into a powerful new antivenom—10 times stronger than existing treatments in lab tests.
body:
Researchers at the University of Maryland have unlocked a life-saving secret hidden in rattlesnake blood: a combination of proteins that can neutralize venom far more effectively than current medical treatments. Led by Distinguished University Professor Sean B. Carroll, the team found that when specific toxin-blocking proteins from western diamondback rattlesnake blood are mixed together, they become about 10 times more potent than sheep-derived rattlesnake antivenom. The findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, point toward a new generation of nature-inspired snakebite treatments that could transform medicine in regions where venomous snakes remain a major threat.

The stakes are enormous. According to the World Health Organization, venomous snakes kill an estimated 80,000 to 140,000 people annually, with hundreds of thousands more left permanently disabled. Existing antivenoms save lives, but they're expensive to produce, variable in quality, and may trigger serious immune reactions. Carroll's team turned the problem on its head: why fight venom with laboratory-made antibodies when snakes themselves have already evolved the perfect defense? In 2022, Carroll's laboratory identified a protein called FETUA-3 in rattlesnake blood that blocks metalloproteinase toxins. The breakthrough came when researchers realized that combining several FETUA proteins together created dramatically stronger protection than any single protein alone.

The work isn't finished. The current study focused on one family of venom toxins, but Carroll and his team are now pursuing the same strategy against other toxin families. He expects nature-based recombinant antivenoms to reach veterinary medicine first, with human treatments potentially following. As snakebite remains one of the world's most neglected tropical diseases, this solution borrowed straight from evolution offers genuine hope for the millions living in danger.
quick_facts: University of Maryland team discovered protein combinations in rattlesnake blood
New antivenom proved 10 times more potent than current treatments in lab tests
Snakebites kill an estimated 80,000 to 140,000 people annually worldwide
Research led by Distinguished Professor Sean B. Carroll, published September 2026
Western diamondback rattlesnake blood provided the key natural defense proteins
